RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria:
Haematuria is blood in the urine. Three questions frame it. (1) Is it really blood? — a positive dipstick needs red cells confirmed on microscopy; a positive dip with no red cells is myoglobin or haemoglobin, and red urine can be beetroot, rifampicin or menstrual contamination. (2) Visible or non-visible, painful or painless? (3) What is the source? — urological (tumour, stone, infection: clots, timing within the stream, colic) versus glomerular (dysmorphic red cells, red-cell casts, proteinuria, hypertension, AKI). The rule that carries the topic: painless visible haematuria in an adult is a urological cancer until proven otherwise (see bladder cancer, renal cell carcinoma), while a nephritic picture is a glomerulonephritis that can cost the kidneys in days (see glomerulonephritis).
🚨Two haematurias are emergencies. Painless visible haematuria — especially aged ≥45, a smoker or with aromatic-amine / dye exposure — is bladder / renal / upper-tract cancer until excluded → 2-week-wait referral for flexible cystoscopy + CT urogram (see bladder cancer). A nephritic picture — haematuria with proteinuria, hypertension and rising creatinine (± red-cell casts, dysmorphic red cells) — is a glomerulonephritis / rapidly progressive GN / vasculitis that can destroy nephrons within days → urgent nephrology and immunology (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, see vasculitis, AKI). Also act on clot retention (catheter / irrigation) and an infected obstructed system (fever + loin pain + obstruction → emergency decompression).

1Triage & screen
🔍Is it really blood?
  • Confirm red cells on microscopy — a positive dipstick alone is not enough
  • Positive dip, no red cells → myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis) or haemoglobinuria (haemolysis)
  • Exclude beetroot, rifampicin, doxorubicin and menstrual contamination
🚩Painless visible haematuria = cancer
  • Bladder cancer (commonest), renal cell carcinoma, upper-tract TCC, prostate — painless and visible is the alarm
  • Risk: age ≥45, smoking, aromatic amines / dyes, prior pelvic radiotherapy, cyclophosphamide
  • 2-week-wait → flexible cystoscopy + CT urogram (see bladder cancer, RCC)
🚩The nephritic emergency
  • Dysmorphic red cells / red-cell casts + proteinuria + hypertension + AKI = a glomerulonephritis
  • Rapidly progressive GN / vasculitis can lose the kidneys in days → urgent nephrology (see glomerulonephritis)
  • Send ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, ANA and consider a renal biopsy (see vasculitis)
🟣Urological, non-malignant
  • Stones: colicky loin-to-groin pain + haematuria (see renal stone disease, loin-to-groin pain)
  • Infection: cystitis / UTI (dysuria, frequency) or pyelonephritis (fever, loin pain) (see UTI, pyelonephritis)
  • BPH, trauma / catheter, schistosomiasis (travel, terminal haematuria) (see BPH)
🟢Localise & characterise
  • Timing in the stream: initial = urethral · terminal = bladder base / prostate · total = bladder / upper tract
  • Clots mean a urological (not glomerular) source; worm-like clots suggest the upper tract
  • Colic → stone · painless → cancer · LUTS → prostate (see LUTS)
🩺Investigate
  • Urine: dipstick + microscopy (red-cell morphology, casts) + MSU culture; ACR / PCR for proteinuria
  • Bloods: U&E / eGFR, FBC, clotting, and BP
  • Imaging: CT urogram (or ultrasound) + flexible cystoscopy; nephrology bloods + biopsy if glomerular
Confirm the blood, then find the source. Prove red cells on microscopy, then split urological (clots, colic, painless visible = cancer) from glomerular (dysmorphic cells, casts, proteinuria, hypertension, AKI). Painless visible haematuria = 2-week-wait; a nephritic picture = urgent nephrology.

Painless vs painful, clots vs casts. Painless visible blood with clots is urological — think cancer first; colic means a stone. Dysmorphic red cells and red-cell casts with proteinuria are glomerular. Confirm the blood is real before chasing either.

At the bedside — confirm the blood, find the source, refer

Visible vs non-visible, painful vs painless, timing in the stream, clots, LUTS, colic, fever, recent sore throat, smoking / occupation / travel, anticoagulants
Examine
Blood pressure, abdomen and flanks (mass, tenderness), a palpable bladder, DRE for the prostate, and oedema (nephrotic / nephritic); dipstick the urine
Investigate

The rules that carry it: prove red cells on microscopy, then decide urological vs glomerular. Painless visible haematuria = cancer until proven otherwise (2-week-wait, cystoscopy + CT urogram). A nephritic picture (proteinuria, hypertension, AKI, casts) = urgent nephrology. Treat infection and stones, and never blame anticoagulation without excluding a lesion.

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain:
Loin pain is pain in the flank / renal angle. The first split is renal / urological vs referred. Renal pain has renal-angle tenderness, urinary features (haematuria, dysuria, see haematuria) and often fever; referred pain comes from the musculoskeletal spine (movement-related), herpes zoster (dermatomal), the chest (basal pneumonia / pleurisy) or the gut. The next split is character: colicky loin-to-groin pain in a patient who cannot lie still is ureteric colic from a stone — its own topic (see loin-to-groin pain) — whereas constant, dull loin pain suggests infection, obstruction, a mass or a referred cause. Two emergencies hide here: an infected obstructed kidney and a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (see AAA).
🚨Two loin pains can kill. Fever + loin pain + an obstructing stone is an infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) — pus under pressure → emergency decompression (nephrostomy / stent) plus antibiotics, before rapid sepsis (see pyelonephritis, stone). A leaking / ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm presents as sudden flank / back pain + collapse or hypotension + a pulsatile mass in an older arteriopath — do not mistake it for renal colic → CT angiogram or straight to theatre (see AAA, pulsatile mass). And obstruction of a single / solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction causes AKI / anuria and needs urgent decompression (see AKI).

1Triage & screen
🔍Renal or referred?
  • Renal: renal-angle tenderness, haematuria / dysuria, fever — think kidney / ureter
  • Musculoskeletal: movement-related, paraspinal tenderness, no urinary features (see back pain)
  • Other referred: herpes zoster (dermatomal ± rash), basal pneumonia / pleurisy (see pneumonia), biliary / bowel
🚩Infected obstructed kidney
  • Fever + loin pain + obstruction (stone) = pyonephrosis — pus under pressure
  • A urological emergency → decompress (nephrostomy / stent) + antibiotics + resuscitate
  • Can become septic quickly; a solitary or bilateral obstruction also causes AKI / anuria (see pyelonephritis)
🚩The AAA mimic
  • Sudden flank / back pain + collapse / hypotension + pulsatile mass in an older arteriopath
  • Leaking / ruptured AAA — classically mistaken for renal colic, especially a first “stone” over 60
  • → CT angiogram or straight to theatre; do not delay (see AAA, pulsatile mass)
🟣Renal / urological causes
  • Pyelonephritis and renal / perinephric abscess; obstruction / hydronephrosis (stone, clot, PUJ, tumour)
  • Renal cell carcinoma (mass, haematuria, weight loss, see RCC); polycystic kidneys (bleed / infection, see inherited kidney disease)
  • Renal infarction / vein thrombosis (AF, nephrotic, thrombophilia, see renal vascular); papillary necrosis
🟢Character & pattern
  • Colicky loin-to-groin, cannot lie still → ureteric stone — its own topic (see loin-to-groin pain)
  • Constant, dull → infection, a mass, obstruction or a referred cause
  • Bilateral loin pain → bilateral obstruction, polycystic kidneys, or medical renal disease
🩺Investigate
  • Urine dipstick + MSU culture; bloods: U&E / eGFR, FBC / CRP, blood cultures if febrile
  • Imaging: CT KUB (stone / obstruction), ultrasound (hydronephrosis), contrast CT for abscess / infarction
  • CT angiogram if an AAA is possible — before labelling a first “stone” in an older patient
Renal or referred, colicky or constant. Renal-angle tenderness + urinary features + fever = a kidney problem; colicky loin-to-groin = a stone (its own topic). Never miss the infected obstructed kidney (fever + obstruction → decompress) or the leaking AAA hiding as a first “renal colic” over 60.

RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin Pain:
Loin-to-groin pain is the classic presentation of ureteric colic — a stone passing down the ureter. It is sudden, severe and colicky (waves), and the patient is characteristically restless and writhing (unlike peritonitis, where they lie still). The pain radiates from the loin to the groin, and on to the scrotum / labia as the stone descends; a stone at the vesicoureteric junction adds bladder irritability (frequency, urgency). Most have haematuria (see haematuria) and vomiting. Confirm with a non-contrast CT KUB. This is a broad topic’s stone half (see loin pain): recognise the colic, but always exclude the mimics — a leaking AAA in the older patient (see AAA) and an ectopic pregnancy in a woman of reproductive age — and act on the infected obstructed stone and AKI.
🚨“Renal colic” is a diagnosis of exclusion in the wrong patient. A first episode over 60, or colic with hypotension or a pulsatile mass, is a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm until the aorta is imaged → CT angiogram, not a CT KUB (see AAA, pulsatile mass). In a woman of reproductive age, do a pregnancy test — an ectopic pregnancy presents as groin / iliac-fossa pain. Fever + an obstructing stone is an infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) → emergency decompression (nephrostomy / stent) + antibiotics (see pyelonephritis); and obstruction of a solitary or both kidneys causes AKI / anuria (see AKI).

1Recognise & exclude
🔍Recognise the colic
  • Sudden, severe, unilateral loin-to-groin pain in waves; the patient is restless / writhing (not still)
  • Radiation tracks the stone: loin → groin → scrotum / labia; a VUJ stone adds frequency / urgency
  • Usually haematuria and vomiting (see haematuria)
🚩Exclude the AAA
  • First colic over 60, hypotension or a pulsatile mass → a leaking AAA, not a stone
  • Image the aorta (CT angiogram) before accepting “renal colic” in an older arteriopath
  • A ruptured AAA is rapidly fatal if mislabelled (see AAA)
🚩Infected obstruction & AKI
  • Fever + an obstructing stone = pyonephrosis → emergency decompression + antibiotics (see pyelonephritis)
  • Obstruction of a solitary or both kidneys → AKI / anuria (see AKI)
  • These override the “wait for the stone to pass” approach
🟣Other mimics
  • Ectopic pregnancy: reproductive-age woman with iliac-fossa / groin pain → pregnancy test
  • Testicular torsion: acute scrotal pain, high-riding testis — examine the scrotum (see testicular torsion, acute scrotal pain)
  • Appendicitis / diverticulitis / biliary depending on side and site
🟢Stone facts that steer it
  • Size: <5 mm usually pass spontaneously; >10 mm rarely do
  • Site: the VUJ is the commonest place to lodge; also PUJ and the pelvic brim
  • Type: calcium oxalate (commonest), uric acid (radiolucent on X-ray, seen on CT), struvite (staghorn, infection), cystine
🩺Investigate
  • Urine dip (blood in ~90%, but absence does not exclude) + MSU; pregnancy test in women
  • Bloods: U&E / eGFR, calcium, urate, FBC / CRP
  • Non-contrast CT KUB is the gold standard; ultrasound in pregnancy / young patients
Restless with loin-to-groin colic and haematuria = a stone — confirm with non-contrast CT KUB. But first exclude the AAA (older, pulsatile, hypotensive) and the ectopic (pregnancy test), and act on the infected obstructed stone (fever → decompress).

Restless writhing is the tell. A patient who cannot lie still has colic (a stone), whereas someone who lies motionless has peritonism. Confirm the stone on CT KUB — but never let a classic story stop you excluding the AAA and the ectopic.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — confirm the colic, exclude the mimics, relieve the pain
History & red flags
Sudden colicky loin-to-groin pain, restlessness, radiation, haematuria, vomiting, LUTS, fever, prior stones, dehydration / diet / gout, pregnancy risk, AAA risk
Examine
Cannot lie still (vs peritonism), renal-angle tenderness, abdomen for a pulsatile mass, the scrotum, observations for sepsis; pregnancy test and urinalysis
Investigate
Non-contrast CT KUB; urine + MSU; U&E, calcium, urate, FBC / CRP; ultrasound if pregnant / young; CT angiogram instead if an AAA is possible
Act
Analgesia (NSAID first-line, e.g. PR diclofenac; opioid if needed) + antiemetic + fluids; small distal stones → expectant + medical expulsive therapy (alpha-blocker); large / failed / obstructing → ureteroscopy / ESWL / PCNL; infected obstruction or AKI → emergency decompression
Then — confirm & prevent
Ureteric stone → non-contrast CT KUBInfected obstruction → CT + cultures → decompressUric acid stone → CT (radiolucent on X-ray) + urateLeaking AAA → CT angiogramEctopic pregnancy → pregnancy test + transvaginal USS
The rules that carry it: restless loin-to-groin colic + haematuria = a stone — confirm on CT KUB. Exclude the AAA and the ectopic. Fever + obstruction = decompress now. Small stones pass with analgesia ± an alpha-blocker; larger ones need intervention — then a metabolic work-up (calcium, urate) and prevention (hydration, diet, ± thiazide / allopurinol / citrate).
